# Feature Factory pipeline

This skill defines the full pipeline for delivering a feature. It composes the
`superpowers` plugin's skills and adds two things superpowers does not: an
**adversarial spec-challenge** step (a fresh Opus subagent that attacks the spec)
and explicit **human review gates** at the points where Sven wants to stay in the
loop.

## Prerequisites

- The **superpowers** plugin must be installed (provides `superpowers:brainstorming`,
  `superpowers:writing-plans`, `superpowers:subagent-driven-development`,
  `superpowers:executing-plans`). If a superpowers skill is missing, say so and stop
  rather than improvising a replacement.
- Stage 6 uses the **`feature-factory:coderabbit-loop`** skill, which drives
  CodeRabbit directly via `gh` - no separate CodeRabbit skill needs to be installed.
- Linear access (the Linear MCP tools, `mcp__*linear*`) for fetching the issue.
- `gh` CLI authenticated, for opening the PR.

## Operating principles

- **Stop at every GATE.** A gate means: present what you have, then wait for an
  explicit human decision. Never cross a gate on your own initiative.
- **One stage at a time.** Announce which stage you are entering and why.
- **Defer, don't reinvent.** Inside a stage, invoke the named superpowers skill and
  let it run. This skill only adds orchestration, the challenge step, and the gates.
- **Persist artifacts.** Keep the spec and plan as files in the repo (the superpowers
  skills already do this) so each stage has a durable input.
- **Respect Sven's conventions** when you (or a subagent) write code: OOP with a
  domain-driven design and dependency injection for Python / TypeScript / C# / Rust;
  a more functional style in Next.js / React to match its design philosophy.

---

## Stage 0 - Intake

1. Resolve the Linear issue from the argument (e.g. `LIN-123`). Use the Linear MCP
   tools to fetch the issue: title, description, comments, labels, linked
   issues/PRs, and acceptance criteria.
2. Restate the issue in 2-4 sentences: the problem, the desired outcome, and any
   constraints you found. Note open questions explicitly.
3. **Move the issue to In Progress.** Use the Linear MCP to transition the issue to
   the team's started / "in progress" workflow state - pick the state whose *type* is
   `started` (commonly named "In Progress", but the exact name varies per team). If
   it is already in that state, leave it. Note the transition in your intake summary.
4. Confirm you are on (or create) an appropriate feature branch. Prefer a
   git worktree (`superpowers:using-git-worktrees`) when one is available, so the
   pipeline does not disturb the user's working tree.

## Stage 1 - Spec (brainstorm)

Invoke **`superpowers:brainstorming`** with the intake summary as the seed. Let it
run its Socratic process and produce the design document / spec. Do not skip its
questions - answer from the Linear context where you can, and surface to the human
any question you cannot answer confidently.

Output of this stage: a saved spec/design document.

## Stage 2 - Adversarial challenge

This replaces Sven's old manual "ask another Opus to challenge the spec" step.

1. Dispatch the **`spec-challenger`** subagent (Opus) with the spec document as
   input. It returns a structured critique with severity-tagged findings
   (BLOCKER / MAJOR / MINOR / QUESTION) and an overall verdict.
2. Triage the critique:
   - **Justified findings** -> fold the fix into the spec. Edit the spec document
     in place.
   - **Unjustified or out-of-scope findings** -> note them with a one-line reason
     for not acting, so the human can see what was considered and rejected.
3. Produce a short changelog: what the challenge surfaced and what you changed.

### >>> GATE 1: spec approval <<<

Present: (a) the revised spec, (b) the challenger's verdict, (c) your changelog of
folded-in vs rejected findings. Then **STOP** and ask Sven to approve, request
further changes, or re-run the challenge (`/challenge-spec`). Do not proceed to
planning until he approves.

## Stage 3 - Implementation plan

Once the spec is approved, invoke **`superpowers:writing-plans`** on the approved
spec. It breaks the design into small, verifiable tasks with exact file paths and
verification steps.

Output: a saved implementation plan. Briefly report the task count and the files it
expects to touch - this feeds the complexity decision next.

## Stage 4 - Implementation

Decide the execution mode from the plan's complexity:

- **Default - subagent-driven.** Use **`superpowers:subagent-driven-development`**.
  Choose this unless the change is clearly trivial.
- **Inline (rare).** Use **`superpowers:executing-plans`** only when the change is
  genuinely small: roughly 1-2 tasks, a single file or tightly scoped area, no new
  abstractions, no cross-cutting concerns.

State which mode you chose and the one-line reason. If it is a borderline call,
ask before starting. Let the chosen superpowers skill drive TDD and per-task review.

When implementation completes, run a final sanity check: tests pass, the diff
matches the plan, no stray debug code.

## Stage 5 - Open the PR

1. Ensure all work is committed and the branch is pushed.
2. Create the PR with `gh pr create`. The PR body should:
   - Link the Linear issue (e.g. `Closes LIN-123` if your Linear<->GitHub link uses
     that, otherwise reference the URL).
   - Summarize the change, the spec decisions, and how it was tested.
3. Report the PR URL.

## Stage 6 - CodeRabbit resolution loop

CodeRabbit reviews the PR automatically. Hand off to the
**`feature-factory:coderabbit-loop`** skill, which runs a **bounded loop of at most
5 rounds**: pull CodeRabbit's threads, fix and reply to justified ones, push back
politely on unjustified ones, resolve all threads, and let CodeRabbit re-review -
stopping when there are no actionable threads left or after 5 rounds.

### >>> GATE 2: loop exit <<<

When the loop ends, **STOP** and report: rounds used, what was changed, which
threads were pushed back on and why, and any items still open (only possible if the
5-round cap was hit). Let Sven decide whether to merge or continue manually.

---

## Quick reference

| Stage | Skill / agent invoked | Gate |
|-------|-----------------------|------|
| 0 Intake | Linear MCP | - |
| 1 Spec | `superpowers:brainstorming` | - |
| 2 Challenge | `spec-challenger` (Opus subagent) | GATE 1: spec approval |
| 3 Plan | `superpowers:writing-plans` | - |
| 4 Implement | `superpowers:subagent-driven-development` (or `:executing-plans`) | - |
| 5 PR | `gh pr create` | - |
| 6 Review loop | `feature-factory:coderabbit-loop` | GATE 2: loop exit |

---

## Post-merge cleanup (run after you merge)

This runs **after GATE 2**, once *you* have merged the PR - merging is always your
decision and is never part of the automated `/ship-feature` run. The `/cleanup`
command invokes this. Goal: get your local checkout back onto an up-to-date base
branch and remove the now-merged branch (and any worktree), without ever touching
unmerged work.

1. **Confirm the PR is merged.** Resolve the PR (from the argument, or the current
   branch's PR) and read its state and branches:
   `gh pr view <pr> --json state,mergedAt,baseRefName,headRefName`. If it is **not**
   merged, stop and say so - delete nothing.
2. **Update the base branch.** Check out the PR's base - `baseRefName`, i.e. whatever
   the PR was merged into (`develop`, `main`, a release branch, ...), not a hardcoded
   default - and pull: `git checkout <base> && git pull`. Your local base now includes
   the merged change.
3. **Remove the worktree, if the pipeline used one.** Find it with `git worktree
   list`, then `git worktree remove <path>` and `git worktree prune`. You must not be
   standing inside the worktree when you remove it.
4. **Delete the merged local branch.** `git branch -d <headRefName>`. If the PR was
   squash- or rebase-merged, git won't recognize the branch as merged and `-d` will
   refuse - because Step 1 already confirmed the PR is merged, use
   `git branch -D <headRefName>` in that case. Never force-delete a branch whose PR
   you have not confirmed merged.
5. **Prune stale refs.** `git fetch --prune` to drop remote-tracking refs for branches
   GitHub deleted on merge.
6. **Report** what changed: base updated, worktree removed (if any), branch deleted,
   refs pruned. If other local branches exist whose PRs are *also* merged, list them
   and offer to clean those too - but only after confirming each one is merged.

"Clean up any local branches" means the **merged** ones. Only ever delete a branch
whose PR is confirmed merged; leave branches with unmerged work alone.

# Using Git Worktrees

## Overview

Ensure work happens in an isolated workspace. Prefer your platform's native worktree tools. Fall back to manual git worktrees only when no native tool is available.

**Core principle:** Detect existing isolation first. Then use native tools. Then fall back to git. Never fight the harness.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the using-git-worktrees skill to set up an isolated workspace."

## Step 0: Detect Existing Isolation

**Before creating anything, check if you are already in an isolated workspace.**

```bash
GIT_DIR=$(cd "$(git rev-parse --git-dir)" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)
GIT_COMMON=$(cd "$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)
BRANCH=$(git branch --show-current)
```

**Submodule guard:** `GIT_DIR != GIT_COMMON` is also true inside git submodules. Before concluding "already in a worktree," verify you are not in a submodule:

```bash
# If this returns a path, you're in a submodule, not a worktree — treat as normal repo
git rev-parse --show-superproject-working-tree 2>/dev/null
```

**If `GIT_DIR != GIT_COMMON` (and not a submodule):** You are already in a linked worktree. Skip to Step 2 (Project Setup). Do NOT create another worktree.

Report with branch state:
- On a branch: "Already in isolated workspace at `<path>` on branch `<name>`."
- Detached HEAD: "Already in isolated workspace at `<path>` (detached HEAD, externally managed). Branch creation needed at finish time."

**If `GIT_DIR == GIT_COMMON` (or in a submodule):** You are in a normal repo checkout.

Has the user already indicated their worktree preference in your instructions? If not, ask for consent before creating a worktree:

> "Would you like me to set up an isolated worktree? It protects your current branch from changes."

Honor any existing declared preference without asking. If the user declines consent, work in place and skip to Step 2.

## Step 1: Create Isolated Workspace

**You have two mechanisms. Try them in this order.**

### 1a. Native Worktree Tools (preferred)

The user has asked for an isolated workspace (Step 0 consent). Do you already have a way to create a worktree? It might be a tool with a name like `EnterWorktree`, `WorktreeCreate`, a `/worktree` command, or a `--worktree` flag. If you do, use it and skip to Step 2.

Native tools handle directory placement, branch creation, and cleanup automatically. Using `git worktree add` when you have a native tool creates phantom state your harness can't see or manage.

Only proceed to Step 1b if you have no native worktree tool available.

### 1b. Git Worktree Fallback

**Only use this if Step 1a does not apply** — you have no native worktree tool available. Create a worktree manually using git.

#### Directory Selection

Follow this priority order. Explicit user preference always beats observed filesystem state.

1. **Check your instructions for a declared worktree directory preference.** If the user has already specified one, use it without asking.

2. **Check for an existing project-local worktree directory:**
   ```bash
   ls -d .worktrees 2>/dev/null     # Preferred (hidden)
   ls -d worktrees 2>/dev/null      # Alternative
   ```
   If found, use it. If both exist, `.worktrees` wins.

3. **If there is no other guidance available**, default to `.worktrees/` at the project root.

#### Safety Verification (project-local directories only)

**MUST verify directory is ignored before creating worktree:**

```bash
git check-ignore -q .worktrees 2>/dev/null || git check-ignore -q worktrees 2>/dev/null
```

**If NOT ignored:** Add to .gitignore, commit the change, then proceed.

**Why critical:** Prevents accidentally committing worktree contents to repository.

#### Create the Worktree

```bash
# Determine path based on chosen location
path="$LOCATION/$BRANCH_NAME"

git worktree add "$path" -b "$BRANCH_NAME"
cd "$path"
```

**Sandbox fallback:** If `git worktree add` fails with a permission error (sandbox denial), tell the user the sandbox blocked worktree creation and you're working in the current directory instead. Then run setup and baseline tests in place.

## Step 2: Project Setup

Auto-detect and run appropriate setup:

```bash
# Node.js
if [ -f package.json ]; then npm install; fi

# Rust
if [ -f Cargo.toml ]; then cargo build; fi

# Python
if [ -f requirements.txt ]; then pip install -r requirements.txt; fi
if [ -f pyproject.toml ]; then poetry install; fi

# Go
if [ -f go.mod ]; then go mod download; fi
```

## Step 3: Verify Clean Baseline

Run tests to ensure workspace starts clean:

```bash
# Use project-appropriate command
npm test / cargo test / pytest / go test ./...
```

**If tests fail:** Report failures, ask whether to proceed or investigate.

**If tests pass:** Report ready.

### Report

```
Worktree ready at <full-path>
Tests passing (<N> tests, 0 failures)
Ready to implement <feature-name>
```

## Quick Reference

| Situation | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| Already in linked worktree | Skip creation (Step 0) |
| In a submodule | Treat as normal repo (Step 0 guard) |
| Native worktree tool available | Use it (Step 1a) |
| No native tool | Git worktree fallback (Step 1b) |
| `.worktrees/` exists | Use it (verify ignored) |
| `worktrees/` exists | Use it (verify ignored) |
| Both exist | Use `.worktrees/` |
| Neither exists | Check instruction file, then default `.worktrees/` |
| Directory not ignored | Add to .gitignore + commit |
| Permission error on create | Sandbox fallback, work in place |
| Tests fail during baseline | Report failures + ask |
| No package.json/Cargo.toml | Skip dependency install |

## Common Mistakes

### Fighting the harness

- **Problem:** Using `git worktree add` when the platform already provides isolation
- **Fix:** Step 0 detects existing isolation. Step 1a defers to native tools.

### Skipping detection

- **Problem:** Creating a nested worktree inside an existing one
- **Fix:** Always run Step 0 before creating anything

### Skipping ignore verification

- **Problem:** Worktree contents get tracked, pollute git status
- **Fix:** Always use `git check-ignore` before creating project-local worktree

### Assuming directory location

- **Problem:** Creates inconsistency, violates project conventions
- **Fix:** Follow priority: explicit instructions > existing project-local directory > default

### Proceeding with failing tests

- **Problem:** Can't distinguish new bugs from pre-existing issues
- **Fix:** Report failures, get explicit permission to proceed

## Red Flags

**Never:**
- Create a worktree when Step 0 detects existing isolation
- Use `git worktree add` when you have a native worktree tool (e.g., `EnterWorktree`). This is the #1 mistake — if you have it, use it.
- Skip Step 1a by jumping straight to Step 1b's git commands
- Create worktree without verifying it's ignored (project-local)
- Skip baseline test verification
- Proceed with failing tests without asking

**Always:**
- Run Step 0 detection first
- Prefer native tools over git fallback
- Follow directory priority: explicit instructions > existing project-local directory > default
- Verify directory is ignored for project-local
- Auto-detect and run project setup
- Verify clean test baseline

# Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs

Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.

Start by understanding the current project context, then ask questions one at a time to refine the idea. Once you understand what you're building, present the design and get user approval.

<HARD-GATE>
Do NOT invoke any implementation skill, write any code, scaffold any project, or take any implementation action until you have presented a design and the user has approved it. This applies to EVERY project regardless of perceived simplicity.
</HARD-GATE>

## Anti-Pattern: "This Is Too Simple To Need A Design"

Every project goes through this process. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config change — all of them. "Simple" projects are where unexamined assumptions cause the most wasted work. The design can be short (a few sentences for truly simple projects), but you MUST present it and get approval.

## Checklist

You MUST create a task for each of these items and complete them in order:

1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Offer the visual companion just-in-time** — NOT upfront. The first time a question would genuinely be clearer shown than described, offer it then (its own message); on approval its browser tab opens for you. If no visual question ever arises, never offer it. See the Visual Companion section below.
3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
4. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation
5. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
6. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` and commit
7. **Spec self-review** — quick inline check for placeholders, contradictions, ambiguity, scope (see below)
8. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file before proceeding
9. **Transition to implementation** — invoke writing-plans skill to create implementation plan

## Process Flow

```dot
digraph brainstorming {
    "Explore project context" [shape=box];
    "Ask clarifying questions" [shape=box];
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" [shape=box];
    "Present design sections" [shape=box];
    "User approves design?" [shape=diamond];
    "Write design doc" [shape=box];
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" [shape=box];
    "User reviews spec?" [shape=diamond];
    "Invoke writing-plans skill" [shape=doublecircle];

    "Explore project context" -> "Ask clarifying questions";
    "Ask clarifying questions" -> "Propose 2-3 approaches";
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" -> "Present design sections";
    "Present design sections" -> "User approves design?";
    "User approves design?" -> "Present design sections" [label="no, revise"];
    "User approves design?" -> "Write design doc" [label="yes"];
    "Write design doc" -> "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)";
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" -> "User reviews spec?";
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Write design doc" [label="changes requested"];
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Invoke writing-plans skill" [label="approved"];
}
```

**The terminal state is invoking writing-plans.** Do NOT invoke frontend-design, mcp-builder, or any other implementation skill. The ONLY skill you invoke after brainstorming is writing-plans.

## The Process

**Understanding the idea:**

- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too
- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria

**Exploring approaches:**

- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
- Lead with your recommended option and explain why

**Presenting the design:**

- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense

**Design for isolation and clarity:**

- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.

**Working in existing codebases:**

- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.

## After the Design

**Documentation:**

- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
- Commit the design document to git

**Spec Self-Review:**
After writing the spec document, look at it with fresh eyes:

1. **Placeholder scan:** Any "TBD", "TODO", incomplete sections, or vague requirements? Fix them.
2. **Internal consistency:** Do any sections contradict each other? Does the architecture match the feature descriptions?
3. **Scope check:** Is this focused enough for a single implementation plan, or does it need decomposition?
4. **Ambiguity check:** Could any requirement be interpreted two different ways? If so, pick one and make it explicit.

Fix any issues inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on.

**User Review Gate:**
After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:

> "Spec written and committed to `<path>`. Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."

Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.

**Implementation:**

- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.

## Key Principles

- **One question at a time** - Don't overwhelm with multiple questions
- **Multiple choice preferred** - Easier to answer than open-ended when possible
- **YAGNI ruthlessly** - Remove unnecessary features from all designs
- **Explore alternatives** - Always propose 2-3 approaches before settling
- **Incremental validation** - Present design, get approval before moving on
- **Be flexible** - Go back and clarify when something doesn't make sense

## Visual Companion

A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode. Accepting the companion means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.

**Offering the companion (just-in-time):** Do NOT offer it upfront. Wait until a question would genuinely be clearer shown than told — a real mockup / layout / diagram question, not merely a UI *topic*. The first time that happens, offer it then, as its own message:
> "This next part might be easier if I show you — I can put together mockups, diagrams, and comparisons in a browser tab as we go. It's still new and can be token-intensive. Want me to? I'll open it for you."

**This offer MUST be its own message.** Only the offer — no clarifying question, summary, or other content. Wait for the user's response. If they accept, start the server with `--open` so their browser opens to the first screen automatically. If they decline, continue text-only and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per-question decision:** Even after the user accepts, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**

- **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
- **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions

A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.

87	    fn model(&self) -> &str {
88	        ""
89	    }
90	}
91	
92	/// The request envelope crossing the model boundary.
93	///
94	/// Carries the conversation, the tools available for the model to
95	/// invoke, and provider-tuning knobs. Field shape is the minimum SMA-314
96	/// needs to drive the loop; SMA-316 / SMA-317 add `tool_choice`,
97	/// `response_format`, `temperature`, and `previous_response_id`.
98	#[derive(Debug, Clone, Default)]
99	#[non_exhaustive]
100	pub struct ModelRequest {
101	    /// The full accumulated conversation so far.
102	    pub messages: Vec<crate::Item>,
103	    /// Tool definitions the model may invoke this turn.
104	    pub tools: Vec<ToolDef>,
105	    /// Provider-tuning knobs.
106	    pub model_settings: ModelSettings,
107	}
108	
109	impl ModelRequest {
110	    /// Construct an empty request. Callers populate fields directly.
111	    pub fn new() -> Self {
112	        Self::default()
113	    }
114	}
115	
116	/// Owned snapshot of a [`crate::Tool`] for cross-async-boundary use
117	/// inside [`ModelRequest`].
118	#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
119	pub struct ToolDef {
120	    /// Identifier the model uses when emitting a tool call.
121	    pub name: String,
122	    /// One-line tool description shown to the model.
123	    pub description: String,
124	    /// JSON Schema for the tool's argument object.
125	    pub schema: serde_json::Value,
126	}
127	
128	/// Provider-tuning knobs.
129	///
130	/// Field shape grew in SMA-316 to cover the surface OpenAI needs;
131	/// SMA-317 (Anthropic) may reshape if Anthropic's protocol demands it.
132	#[derive(Debug, Clone, Default)]
133	#[non_exhaustive]
134	pub struct ModelSettings {
135	    /// Sampling temperature. Provider-defined default when unset.
136	    pub temperature: Option<f32>,
137	    /// Nucleus-sampling top-p. Provider-defined default when unset.
138	    pub top_p: Option<f32>,
139	    /// Cap on output tokens per response. Maps to `max_tokens` on
140	    /// OpenAI Chat and to `max_output_tokens` on OpenAI Responses.
141	    pub max_output_tokens: Option<u32>,
142	    /// Caller's tool-selection preference. See [`ToolChoice`].
143	    pub tool_choice: Option<ToolChoice>,
144	    /// Caller's response-shape preference. See [`ResponseFormat`].
145	    pub response_format: Option<ResponseFormat>,
146	    /// OpenAI Responses-API server-side state token. **Caller-managed:**
147	    /// when set, callers MUST trim [`ModelRequest::messages`] to only
148	    /// the items added since the response identified by this id. The
149	    /// provider passes `messages` through as-is — it does not filter.
150	    /// Integration with [`crate::LlmAgent`]'s automatic conversation
151	    /// accumulation is out of scope for SMA-316; see follow-up ticket.
152	    /// Ignored by non-OpenAI-Responses providers.
153	    pub previous_response_id: Option<String>,
154	}
155	
156	impl ModelSettings {
157	    /// Construct default model settings (all fields unset).
158	    pub fn new() -> Self {
159	        Self::default()
160	    }
161	}
162	
163	/// Streaming union — token / reasoning / tool-call deltas, usage snapshots, finish.
164	///
165	/// See ADR-1 (*Single Model trait with capabilities flags*).
166	#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
167	#[non_exhaustive]
168	pub enum ModelEvent {
169	    /// A chunk of assistant text.
170	    TokenDelta {
171	        /// The text fragment.
172	        text: String,
173	    },
174	    /// A chunk of reasoning/scratchpad text (for providers that emit it
175	    /// separately from the assistant text channel).
176	    ReasoningDelta {
177	        /// The text fragment.
178	        text: String,
179	    },
180	    /// A partial tool call. `name` is `Some` on the first delta for a given
181	    /// `call_id`, then `None` on subsequent deltas as `args_delta` chunks
182	    /// arrive.
183	    ToolCallDelta {
184	        /// Provider-assigned identifier for the call.
185	        call_id: String,
186	        /// Tool name; `Some` on the first delta only.
187	        name: Option<String>,
188	        /// JSON-encoded argument fragment.
189	        args_delta: String,
190	    },
191	    /// Token-usage snapshot emitted by the provider.
192	    ///
193	    /// **Ordering contract** (per [`Model::invoke`] docs): a `Usage` MAY
194	    /// appear anywhere in the stream. `Finish` is always terminal.
195	    /// OpenAI emits one `Usage` immediately before `Finish`; Anthropic emits
196	    /// updates that are **cumulative within the response** (each carries the
197	    /// running total, not a per-chunk delta).
198	    ///
199	    /// **Last-wins contract:** each `Usage` is a complete snapshot, so a
200	    /// consumer tracking a turn's total retains the **last** `Usage` seen and
201	    /// never sums `Usage` events *within* a turn. The agent loop then sums these
202	    /// per-turn finals **across** turns for the run total (SMA-402); a provider
203	    /// emitting true per-chunk deltas would violate this and under-count, so
204	    /// implementations MUST emit cumulative-within-turn usage.
205	    Usage {
206	        /// Prompt / input tokens consumed.
207	        input_tokens: u32,
208	        /// Completion / output tokens generated.
209	        output_tokens: u32,
210	        /// Cached input tokens (OpenAI prompt-caching, Anthropic
211	        /// ephemeral cache). `None` when the provider does not report
212	        /// caching or none was hit.
213	        cached_input_tokens: Option<u32>,
214	        /// Reasoning tokens (OpenAI o1/o3/gpt-5; Anthropic extended
215	        /// thinking). `None` when the provider does not separate
216	        /// reasoning from output tokens.
217	        reasoning_tokens: Option<u32>,
218	    },
219	    /// Terminal event for a single response.
220	    Finish {
221	        /// Why the response ended.
222	        reason: FinishReason,
223	    },
224	}
225	
226	/// Why a single model response stopped emitting tokens.
227	#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
228	#[non_exhaustive]
229	pub enum FinishReason {
230	    /// Natural stop.
231	    Stop,
232	    /// Hit the model's max-output-tokens limit.
233	    Length,
234	    /// Model emitted tool calls and is awaiting their results.
235	    ToolCalls,
236	    /// Provider's content filter rejected the response.
237	    ContentFilter,
238	    /// Provider-specific stop reason that does not map to a known variant.
239	    Other(String),
240	}
241	
242	/// Provider capability flags. See ADR-1.
243	///
244	/// Capability flags inform the agent loop's behavior (e.g. whether to use
245	/// JSON-mode structured output, whether to expect parallel tool calls).
246	/// They are stable per [`Model`] instance.
247	#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, Default, PartialEq, Eq)]
248	#[non_exhaustive]
249	pub struct ModelCapabilities {

# paigasus-helikon-runtime-temporal

The Temporal-backed durable runtime for the [Paigasus Helikon](https://github.com/SMK1085/paigasus-helikon) AI SDK — a Rust SDK for building AI agents.

> **Not yet implemented.** This crate is a pre-published `0.0.0` name-claim placeholder: the name is reserved on crates.io and the [`paigasus-helikon`](https://crates.io/crates/paigasus-helikon) facade exposes a `runtime-temporal` feature for it, but the crate is currently empty. **Don't depend on it yet** — the real implementation lands in a future release.

# paigasus-helikon-runtime-agentcore

The AWS Bedrock AgentCore runtime for the [Paigasus Helikon](https://github.com/SMK1085/paigasus-helikon) AI SDK — a Rust SDK for building AI agents.

> **Not yet implemented.** This crate is a pre-published `0.0.0` name-claim placeholder: the name is reserved on crates.io and the [`paigasus-helikon`](https://crates.io/crates/paigasus-helikon) facade exposes a `runtime-agentcore` feature for it, but the crate is currently empty. **Don't depend on it yet** — the real implementation lands in a future release.

# AWS Bedrock AgentCore Runtime — custom-container service contract (verified July 2026)

## 1. HTTP protocol contract (`serverProtocol: HTTP`)

Source: [HTTP protocol contract](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-http-protocol-contract.html), [service contract overview](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-service-contract.html), [Get started without the CLI](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/getting-started-custom.html)

- **Bind**: host `0.0.0.0`, **port 8080**. Platform: ARM64 container (required).
- **`POST /invocations`** (REQUIRED): JSON in, JSON or SSE out.
  - Request: `Content-Type: application/json`, arbitrary JSON body — the InvokeAgentRuntime `payload` is passed through verbatim (the body shape like `{"prompt": ...}` or `{"input": {...}}` is your application's convention, not enforced by AWS).
  - Non-streaming response: `Content-Type: application/json`, any JSON body.
  - Streaming response: **SSE with `Content-Type: text/event-stream`**, standard `data: {...}\n\n` frames per the WHATWG SSE spec. This is the only documented streaming mechanism on `/invocations` (plus optional WebSocket, below). The service passes the stream through to the InvokeAgentRuntime caller (response Content-Type is propagated).
- **`GET /ping`** (REQUIRED): `Content-Type: application/json`, HTTP 200 when healthy. Body:
  - `{"status": "Healthy"}` — ready for new work, or
  - `{"status": "HealthyBusy"}` — busy with async/background tasks; while `HealthyBusy`, the session is considered active and is kept alive past the idle timeout.
  - Optional field `time_of_last_update` (Unix seconds): set **only when status actually changes**. AWS explicitly warns that advancing it on every ping prevents idle timeout from ever firing (sessions persist until maxLifetime and can exhaust session quota). Omitting it is fine — the platform tracks status changes itself. ([long-running agents doc](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-long-run.html); real-world gotcha history in [bedrock-agentcore-sdk-python#471](https://github.com/aws/bedrock-agentcore-sdk-python/issues/471))
  - Value casing: the contract page uses `Healthy`/`HealthyBusy` (the getting-started page's `{"status": "healthy"}` example suggests plain-healthy lowercase is tolerated for the simple case, but `HealthyBusy` semantics are only documented in the exact casing — emit exact casing).
  - The ping poll interval is **not documented** by AWS (community examples suggest ~30 s; unverified). An unhealthy/blocked ping gets the compute deemed unhealthy and terminated, so `/ping` must never be blocked by invocation work (AWS explicitly warns single-threaded servers get killed at 15 min when the ping handler is starved).
- **`GET /ws`** (OPTIONAL, same port 8080): WebSocket upgrade endpoint for bidirectional streaming; text/binary frames, 64 KB max frame, 250 frames/s per connection, session bound via `X-Amzn-Bedrock-AgentCore-Runtime-Session-Id` header on the upgrade request.
- **Auth responses**: OAuth-configured runtimes get 401 + `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="..."` from the service when Authorization is missing; SigV4-configured runtimes get 403 `ACCESS_DENIED`. This is handled at the service edge, not by your container.

## 2. MCP protocol contract (`serverProtocol: MCP`)

Source: [MCP protocol contract](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-mcp-protocol-contract.html), [Deploy MCP servers](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-mcp.html), [Stateful MCP features](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/mcp-stateful-features.html)

- **Bind**: host `0.0.0.0`, **port 8000**, path **`/mcp`** (POST). ARM64 required.
- **Transport**: MCP **streamable-HTTP transport is required** (no stdio, no legacy HTTP+SSE dual-endpoint). JSON-RPC bodies; the server may respond with `application/json` or `text/event-stream` — both are supported/passed through.
- **Statelessness**: stateless mode (`stateless_http=True` in FastMCP terms) is the **default recommendation**, not an absolute requirement — stateful MCP servers are also supported (needed for elicitation, sampling, progress notifications).
- **`Mcp-Session-Id` handling** (critical for a Rust implementation):
  - Stateless mode: **the platform generates `Mcp-Session-Id` and injects it into the request to your server**. Your server MUST accept an unknown, platform-provided `Mcp-Session-Id` without rejecting it (a spec-strict server that 404s unknown session IDs breaks). The platform echoes the ID to the client; the client must resend it for microVM affinity.
  - Stateful mode: client initializes without the header; platform returns one; client must resend it — it carries both session state and microVM stickiness.
  - In both modes the service always returns `Mcp-Session-Id` to the caller; requests without a consistent ID may each land on a fresh microVM (cold start each time).
- `/ping` is **not** part of the MCP contract page's path requirements — only `/mcp` is specified for MCP runtimes. (Whether the platform still probes container health another way is undocumented; the bedrock-agentcore Python SDK's MCP mode serves only `/mcp`.)
- InvokeAgentRuntime passes `Mcp-Session-Id` and `Mcp-Protocol-Version` headers through end-to-end ([InvokeAgentRuntime API](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/APIReference/API_InvokeAgentRuntime.html)).

## 3. Sessions, headers, limits

Source: [isolated sessions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-sessions.html), [quotas](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/bedrock-agentcore-limits.html), [LifecycleConfiguration](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore-control/latest/APIReference/API_LifecycleConfiguration.html), [InvokeAgentRuntime](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/APIReference/API_InvokeAgentRuntime.html)

- **One dedicated microVM per session** (Firecracker-style; CPU/memory/filesystem isolated). MicroVM terminated + memory sanitized after session end. Session states: Active / Idle / Stopped; a Stopped session revives on next invoke with a fresh compute (same sessionId stays valid until the runtime ARN is deleted).
- **Session header by protocol**: HTTP/A2A/AG-UI → `X-Amzn-Bedrock-AgentCore-Runtime-Session-Id`; MCP → `Mcp-Session-Id`. `runtimeSessionId` must be **33–256 chars**.
- **Other invoke headers passed through**: `X-Amzn-Bedrock-AgentCore-Runtime-User-Id` (needs `bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntimeForUser` too), `X-Amzn-Trace-Id`, `traceparent`, `tracestate`, `baggage`, `Mcp-Protocol-Version`.
- **Custom headers**: `requestHeaderConfiguration.requestHeaderAllowlist` on CreateAgentRuntime — up to **20 header names**, pattern `[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_-]{0,255}`, passed through to the container ([RequestHeaderConfiguration](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore-control/latest/APIReference/API_RequestHeaderConfiguration.html)).
- **Lifecycle**: `idleRuntimeSessionTimeout` default **900 s (15 min)**, range 60–28800; `maxLifetime` default **28800 s (8 h)**, range 60–28800. `StopRuntimeSession` API for explicit termination.
- **Hard limits** (quotas page, none adjustable): payload **100 MB** request/response (API constraint: payload 0–100,000,000 bytes); synchronous request timeout **15 min**; streaming connection max **60 min**; streaming chunk max **10 MB**; async job (HealthyBusy) max **8 h**; WebSocket frame 64 KB; session storage (optional persistent FS) 1 GB.
- **Rates** (post-June-2026 increases, adjustable): 200 TPS InvokeAgentRuntime per agent; 400 new sessions/min per endpoint (container); 5,000 concurrent active sessions (us-east-1/us-west-2), 2,500 elsewhere ([release notes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html), [whats-new](https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/07/amazon-bedrock-agentcore-increases-default-runtime-quota-limits/)).

## 4. Container requirements

- **`linux/arm64` mandatory** (all protocols). Image must live in **ECR** (private ECR in same region). Max **Docker image size 2 GB**. Max hardware per session: **2 vCPU / 8 GB** (not adjustable, allocation is managed — you don't pick a size). Sources: [getting-started-custom](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/getting-started-custom.html), [quotas](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/bedrock-agentcore-limits.html).
- **Cold start**: not stated as an SLA in AWS docs. AWS re:Post staff article ["Minimizing startup latency"](https://repost.aws/articles/ARCJIn3t7aRC2FxiRTV1SuCA/minimizing-startup-latency-with-amazon-bedrock-agentcore-runtime) + community sources put container cold starts at roughly **2–5 s** platform-side (microVM provision + image pull) plus your app init; warm same-session invokes are sub-second overhead. Treat the numbers as indicative, not contractual. (A Rust/axum image will be near the best case — tiny image, no interpreter startup.)
- Since Nov 2025 there is also a **direct code deployment** path (ZIP, Python/Node managed runtimes, 250 MB compressed) — not applicable to a Rust shim; containers remain the Rust path.

## 5. `protocolConfiguration` / A2A status

- `ProtocolConfiguration.serverProtocol` valid values: **`MCP | HTTP | A2A | AGUI`** ([ProtocolConfiguration API](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore-control/latest/APIReference/API_ProtocolConfiguration.html)). Default when omitted is HTTP.
- **A2A is GA, not preview**: AgentCore went GA 2025-10-13 with A2A Runtime support in the same launch ([whats-new](https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2025/10/amazon-bedrock-agentcore-available/), [AWS ML blog A2A post](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/introducing-agent-to-agent-protocol-support-in-amazon-bedrock-agentcore-runtime/)). A2A contract: **port 9000, mount path `/` (root)**, JSON-RPC 2.0, agent-card discovery ([A2A protocol contract](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-a2a-protocol-contract.html)).
- **AG-UI** (`AGUI`) was added later (release-notes entry March 2026): port 8080, `/invocations` (SSE) + `/ws` ([AG-UI contract](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-agui-protocol-contract.html)).
- CreateAgentRuntime also takes `environmentVariables` (max 50), `networkConfiguration` (`PUBLIC` or VPC mode with subnets/SGs), `lifecycleConfiguration`, `filesystemConfigurations` (up to 5 mounts, S3 Files/EFS — May 2026 feature), `authorizerConfiguration` (IAM/SigV4 default, or JWT/OAuth), `roleArn` (required). Response includes auto-provisioned `workloadIdentityDetails.workloadIdentityArn` ([CreateAgentRuntime](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore-control/latest/APIReference/API_CreateAgentRuntime.html)).

## 6. CDK support (as of mid-2026)

**There is a stable L2 in `aws-cdk-lib` — not L1-only.** The constructs graduated from `@aws-cdk/aws-bedrock-agentcore-alpha` into **`aws-cdk-lib/aws-bedrockagentcore`** (all except Policy, per the alpha module's notice); L1 `CfnRuntime` also exists in the same module. Sources: [aws-cdk-lib.aws_bedrockagentcore module](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cdk/api/v2/docs/aws-cdk-lib.aws_bedrockagentcore-readme.html), [Runtime construct](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cdk/api/v2/docs/aws-cdk-lib.aws_bedrockagentcore.Runtime.html), [CfnRuntime](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cdk/api/v2/docs/aws-cdk-lib.aws_bedrockagentcore.CfnRuntime.html), [alpha npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@aws-cdk/aws-bedrock-agentcore-alpha).

Minimal TypeScript (verbatim shape from the module README, imports corrected):

```typescript
import * as ecr from "aws-cdk-lib/aws-ecr";
import * as agentcore from "aws-cdk-lib/aws-bedrockagentcore";

const repository = ecr.Repository.fromRepositoryName(this, "Repo", "my-agent");

const runtime = new agentcore.Runtime(this, "MyAgentRuntime", {
  runtimeName: "myAgent",
  agentRuntimeArtifact: agentcore.AgentRuntimeArtifact.fromEcrRepository(repository, "v1.0.0"),
  // defaults: ProtocolType.HTTP, public network, IAM (SigV4) auth, auto-created execution role
});

const prodEndpoint = runtime.addEndpoint("production", { version: "1" });
```

`RuntimeProps` verified: `agentRuntimeArtifact` (also `fromAsset`/`fromImageUri`/`fromCodeAsset`/`fromS3` factories), `protocolConfiguration?: ProtocolType` (default `ProtocolType.HTTP`), `networkConfiguration?` (`RuntimeNetworkConfiguration.usingPublicNetwork()` / `.usingVpc(...)`), `authorizerConfiguration?`, `lifecycleConfiguration?`, `environmentVariables?`, `executionRole?`, `tracingEnabled?`. **Caveat**: I verified the `protocolConfiguration` prop and its `ProtocolType` enum with HTTP default; that `ProtocolType.MCP` is the exact member name for MCP is high-confidence but I did not see it verbatim in a doc quote — check the enum before hardcoding.

## 7. Observability / misc for a Rust shim

Source: [observability-configure](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/observability-configure.html)

- Runtime-hosted agents are auto-instrumented **only** if they run the ADOT SDK (Python: `opentelemetry-instrument` + `aws-opentelemetry-distro`). The runtime **sets default ADOT OTEL environment variables in the container** — verified indirectly: setting `DISABLE_ADOT_OBSERVABILITY=true` "unsets the AgentCore runtime's default ADOT environment variables". The exact injected list is not enumerated for the hosted case; the documented outside-runtime equivalents (same pipeline) are: `AGENT_OBSERVABILITY_ENABLED=true`, `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL=http/protobuf`, `OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER=otlp`, `OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES=service.name=...,aws.log.group.names=/aws/bedrock-agentcore/runtimes/<agent-id>,cloud.resource_id=...`, `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_LOGS_HEADERS=x-aws-log-group=...,x-aws-log-stream=runtime-logs,x-aws-metric-namespace=bedrock-agentcore`. A Rust shim wanting traces in CloudWatch GenAI Observability should read the standard `OTEL_*` env vars via `opentelemetry-otlp` (http/protobuf) and propagate `traceparent`/`baggage`/`X-Amzn-Trace-Id` from inbound requests; requires the one-time CloudWatch Transaction Search enablement. stdout/stderr go to the auto-created CloudWatch log group regardless.
- **Workload identity**: each runtime automatically gets a workload identity (`workloadIdentityDetails` in Create/Get responses); container code exchanges it via AgentCore Identity (`GetWorkloadAccessToken*`) for OAuth/API-key egress. AWS credentials for `roleArn` are available in the container through the standard SDK credential chain (Rust: `aws-config` just works).
- **Timing obligations**: no documented deadline for the first successful `/ping` after container start, and **no documented ping poll interval**; but an unresponsive `/ping` ⇒ compute deemed unhealthy ⇒ terminated. Keep `/ping` on a never-blocked path.
- **Graceful shutdown**: AWS documents **no SIGTERM/grace-period contract** for session termination (idle timeout, maxLifetime, StopRuntimeSession, unhealthy). Treat termination as abrupt; handle SIGTERM defensively but don't rely on it. (Community reports describe the platform backing up session storage before kill; unverified.)

## Verified vs inferred

**Verified from AWS docs**: ports 8080/8000/9000 + paths per protocol; ARM64; ECR; `/invocations` + `/ping` shapes incl. Healthy/HealthyBusy and `time_of_last_update` semantics; SSE `text/event-stream` streaming; MCP streamable-HTTP + stateless-default + platform-injected `Mcp-Session-Id`; all headers; 33-char session ID; 100 MB payload / 15 min sync / 60 min stream / 8 h async / 2 GB image / 2 vCPU-8 GB; lifecycle defaults 15 min/8 h (60–28800 s range); `serverProtocol: MCP|HTTP|A2A|AGUI`; A2A GA Oct 2025; CDK L2 `Runtime` in `aws-cdk-lib/aws-bedrockagentcore`; `DISABLE_ADOT_OBSERVABILITY`; requestHeaderAllowlist (≤20).

**Inferred/uncertain**: ping poll interval (~30 s, community); cold start 2–5 s (AWS re:Post article, not an SLA); exact injected OTEL env-var list for hosted containers; SIGTERM behavior; exact CDK `ProtocolType.MCP` member name; whether `/ping` is probed at all for MCP-protocol runtimes.

## Contract checklist — Rust axum server

**HTTP variant** (`serverProtocol: HTTP`):
1. Bind `0.0.0.0:8080`; image built `--platform linux/arm64`, pushed to ECR (< 2 GB).
2. `POST /invocations`: accept arbitrary JSON up to 100 MB; reply `application/json` (complete ≤ 15 min) or `text/event-stream` SSE (`data: <json>\n\n`, chunks ≤ 10 MB, stream ≤ 60 min); flush frames eagerly (no buffering).
3. `GET /ping`: always-responsive (own task, never blocked by invocation work); 200 + `{"status":"Healthy"}` or `{"status":"HealthyBusy"}` (exact casing); include `time_of_last_update` only on genuine status transitions, or omit entirely.
4. Read `X-Amzn-Bedrock-AgentCore-Runtime-Session-Id` (and optional `X-Amzn-Bedrock-AgentCore-Runtime-User-Id`, `traceparent`, `baggage`, allowlisted custom headers) per request; one process instance == one session (microVM), so in-memory state is per-session by construction.
5. Return `HealthyBusy` while background work runs (keeps session alive up to 8 h); revert to `Healthy` when done so idle timeout can reclaim the microVM.
6. Tolerate abrupt kill (no SIGTERM guarantee); anything durable goes to external storage/AgentCore Memory/session storage mount.
7. Optional: `GET /ws` WebSocket upgrade on the same port (64 KB frames, 250 fps).

**MCP variant** (`serverProtocol: MCP`):
1. Bind `0.0.0.0:8000`; serve MCP **streamable-HTTP** at `POST /mcp` (JSON-RPC 2.0; also handle `GET`/`DELETE /mcp` per the streamable-HTTP spec for SSE channel/session teardown if you implement them).
2. Respond `application/json` or `text/event-stream` per request's `Accept`.
3. Run **stateless**: accept any inbound `Mcp-Session-Id` (platform-generated, unknown to you) — never 400/404 an unrecognized session ID; don't require `initialize` before other calls to have happened on the same connection.
4. Echo/emit `Mcp-Session-Id` per streamable-HTTP rules; the platform handles client-facing session affinity.
5. Same container rules: arm64, ECR, ≤ 2 GB, 100 MB payload cap, abrupt-kill tolerance. `/ping` not part of the documented MCP contract (implementing a trivial one anyway is harmless and cheap insurance).

Key sources: [runtime-service-contract](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-service-contract.html) · [runtime-http-protocol-contract](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-http-protocol-contract.html) · [runtime-mcp-protocol-contract](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-mcp-protocol-contract.html) · [runtime-sessions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-sessions.html) · [runtime-long-run](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-long-run.html) · [bedrock-agentcore-limits](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/bedrock-agentcore-limits.html) · [CreateAgentRuntime](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore-control/latest/APIReference/API_CreateAgentRuntime.html) · [InvokeAgentRuntime](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/APIReference/API_InvokeAgentRuntime.html) · [getting-started-custom](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/getting-started-custom.html) · [CDK aws_bedrockagentcore](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cdk/api/v2/docs/aws-cdk-lib.aws_bedrockagentcore-readme.html) · [release-notes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html) · [observability-configure](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/observability-configure.html) · [A2A GA whats-new](https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2025/10/amazon-bedrock-agentcore-available/) · [startup-latency re:Post article](https://repost.aws/articles/ARCJIn3t7aRC2FxiRTV1SuCA/minimizing-startup-latency-with-amazon-bedrock-agentcore-runtime) · [sdk-python#471 ping gotcha](https://github.com/aws/bedrock-agentcore-sdk-python/issues/471)</result>

README/crate-docs wording (verified in `crates/sdk/src/lib.rs` and `crates/sdk/README.md`): *"This crate contains a Public Preview Rust SDK. … The SDK is in Public Preview and under active development.
